His days were measured not in hours but in the rhythm of the sea, the creak of the great lens, and the silence that pressed against the glass of the watch room. He was a man of few words, and the only conversation he ever had was with the gulls that circled above the tower.

He had kept a ledger for decades, noting the weather, the ships that passed, and the strange things the sea delivered to his shore. # The Keeper of Harrow Point

The bottle came in on a Tuesday, which was the worst kind of day for miracles.

Eamon Voss had kept the Harrow Point light for thirty-one years. He knew the rhythm of the sea the way a pianist knows a sonata—where the swells would crest, where the undertow would pull, where the rocks would bite. He knew the gulls, the fog, the particular silence that fell over the headland when the barometer dropped. He did not know what to do with a green glass bottle, barnacled and salt-crusted, that the tide had deposited at the base of the tower like a small, stubborn secret.

He carried it inside, set it on the workbench beside his logbook and his cold cup of tea, and turned it over in his thick fingers. The cork was swollen with years of brine. It took him four minutes and a flathead screwdriver to free it.

Inside, rolled tight as a sleeping thing, was a strip of paper.

He unrolled it carefully, the way you'd handle a wounded bird. The ink had faded to the color of old bruises, but the words were legible:

*To whoever finds this—I am Maren. I am writing this because I am afraid of what I will do tomorrow, and I need someone to know that I was not always this. I was kind once. I was the girl who left bread on the windowsill for the stray cats. I was the girl who cried at the end of films. I am putting this in the sea because the sea does not judge. The sea only carries. If you are reading this, I am already gone, or I am already changed. I hope it is the first. I hope the sea was kinder to me than I was to myself.*

*—Maren, 1987*

Eamon set the paper down.

# The Keeper of Harrow Point

The bottle washed up on a Tuesday, which was the kind of day that suited it. Grey and flat, the sea the color of wet slate, the wind carrying no more than a whisper through the iron railings of the cliff path.

Eamon Voss had kept the Harrow Point light for eleven years. Eleven years of climbing the one hundred and twelve steps each evening, trimming the wick, polishing the great Fresnel lens until it caught the last of the sun and threw it back in a slow, golden wheel. Eleven years of talking to the gulls, of mending nets for the fishermen below, of watching the same stretch of Atlantic churn and churn and churn.

He found the bottle wedged between two rocks near the base of the tower, half-buried in kelp and sand. It was green glass, old-fashioned, with a cork stopper sealed in wax the color of dried blood. Inside, a rolled slip of paper.

He should have logged it. The Coast Guard wanted every found object catalogued, tagged, shipped to a warehouse in the city where it would sit in a drawer for a decade. But Eamon was not a man who followed procedure well. He'd never been good at procedure.

He carried it up the one hundred and twelve steps. He set it on the workbench beside his cold tea and his half-eaten tin of biscuits. He stared at it for a long time.

Then he broke the wax.

The paper was soft with salt and age, the ink faded to a rusty brown. The handwriting was small, cramped, the letters pressed hard into the page as though the writer had been in a hurry or in fear.

# The Keeper of Harrow Point

The bottle washed up on a Tuesday, which was the kind of day that made Elias Vane feel the weight of the lighthouse pressing down on his shoulders. Gray sky. Gray sea. The same gray he'd worn for eleven years, from the salt-stiffened wool of his coat to the film of it in his eyes.

He was mending the net along the eastern rocks when he saw it—green glass, half-buried in the kelp, catching what little light the clouds allowed. He pulled it free. The cork was swollen with brine but held. Inside, a rolled slip of paper, dark with age.

Elias sat on the cold stone, his hands trembling in a way he hadn't felt since Margaret left. He pried the cork free with his thumbnail and unrolled the paper.

*To whoever finds this: I am Thomas Wren, keeper of Harrow Point Light, 1923. The storms are worse this year. I have not spoken to another soul in four months. If you are reading this, know that the light still burns. Know that I am still here. Know that the sea does not take everything, even if it feels like it does.*

*—T.W.*
